Keywords: breath monitoring | capacitive sensing | E-Textiles | sensors | stretch sensing | wearable sensing

ABSTRACT Designing garments that effectively capture human movements demands a focus on the wearer’s comfort and freedom of motion. Electronic textile (e-Textile) sensors offer a promising avenue due to their soft and flexible properties. However, these sensors are most responsive to large motions, as their precision is usually relatively low compared to other sensing solutions. Furthermore, eTextile sensors that measure physical force or deformation often require the sensing element itself to undergo deformation and be subject to force. This leads to degradation of the sensor due to repeated mechanical strain. To address these issues, a novel all-textile mechanical capacitive sensor design is presented. This sensor is optimized for measuring subtle movements, such as thoracic wall movements, in breath monitoring. The design is more robust than other e-Textile sensing approaches, as the deforming textile elements are separated from the sensing element. This design choice results in sensors with improved signal response, higher accuracy, and longer cycle life than the other comparable textile sensors. In this paper, we share the design and implementation guidelines, in vitro measurements (such as evaluation of the effects of electrode shape and size and cycle life tests), and multiple in vivo measurements of sensor prototypes.

The interlocking loop structure of knit fabrics can serve as the basis for stretch-sensitive structures [21], while the compliance of nonwoven fabrics can support compression-sensitive structures [22]. From a mechanical perspective, e-Textile sensor design begins by defining how the textile deforms: it may stretch, compress, shear, change contact area, or shift the relative position of materials.

Interactive garments increasingly function as interfaces that tightly couple people and technology [1–4]. While early interactive garments often augmented users through wearable output, such as displays [5], or input, such as touch sensors [6], recent systems are designed to integrate more closely into bodily activity and expressive movement [7–13]. This shift places stronger demands on garment-integrated sensing technologies: sensors must be soft, compliant, non-restrictive, and capable of capturing subtle body movements and small garment deformations [14–16].

From an electrical perspective, this deformation must then be converted into a measurable signal. Resistive textile sensors measure changes in resistance caused by elongation of conductive yarns or fabrics, contact between conductive elements, or compression of compliant fabrics [21–24]. Capacitive textile sensors instead measure changes in capacitance caused by electrode spacing, dielectric properties, contact geometry, or electrode overlap. Other capacitive textile stretch sensors for motion tracking use silicone-textile composites and interdigital conductive-knit sensors [26, 27]. Recent work on robust capacitive pressure sensors further shows how porous dielectric layers and protective textile/polymer architectures can improve sensitivity, durability, and environmental resilience for pressure monitoring in demanding conditions [28].

This coupling between mechanical deformation and electrical readout is also a central challenge. The same textile structure often has to provide both the desired mechanical behavior and the desired electrical response. As a result, material properties that are beneficial for softness and integration can introduce limitations in sensing: knitted structures can produce nonlinear stretch responses [23], while the slow recovery behavior of non-woven fabrics can result in pressure sensors with high hysteresis [22]. More generally, repeated deformation of the electrically active textile structure can mechanically stress conductive pathways or electrodes, negatively affecting cycle life [23] and sensing stability over time [24].

These limitations become particularly important for smallamplitude, garment-integrated movements, where the signal of interest may be obscured by nonlinear material responses, hysteresis, drift, and other confounding effects caused by stretch, compression, shear, proximity, contact area, and garment fit. In such cases, sensing fidelity depends not only on the electrical readout principle, but also on how precisely the deformation is mechanically designed. Recent mechanically engineered strain sensors based on predefined conductive cracks demonstrate one response to this problem: controlling the deformation pathway can improve sensitivity and linearity by making conductivepathway deformation more predictable [29].

Measurement of the capacitance between the two conductive pads provides a robust, high-resolution, and linear measure of stretch. In both designs, separating mechanically and electrically functional elements leads to more robust designs. Instead of optimizing one fabric for both mechanical and electrical functionality, designers can choose fabrics specifically for their mechanical properties and separate conductive fabrics for their electrical properties. The resulting sensors no longer experience degradation of electrical functionality due to mechanical stress. We constructed six sensors using Design A in three sizes: 1 × 3 cm, 3 × 3 cm, and 5 × 3 cm. For each size, one sensor had two rectangular electrodes (rr), and the other had a rectangular and a triangular electrode (rt) (see Figure 1c). For Design B, we built two sensors, both 3 × 3 cm – one with two rectangular electrodes and one with a rectangular and a triangular electrode (see Figure S1). Throughout the paper, sensor labels follow the format [electrode geometry]-[W × L]-[design]. The electrodegeometry prefix describes the pair of capacitive electrodes: rr denotes a rectangular–rectangular electrode pair, and rt denotes a rectangular–triangular electrode pair. W and L denote the electrode width and length, respectively, in centimeters. The design suffix denotes the fabrication approach: A refers to the bonded textile-composite design using engineered stretch and non-stretch materials with encapsulated electrodes, whereas B refers to the simplified off-the-shelf elastic design. For example, rr-3 × 3-A denotes a Design A sensor with a rectangular– rectangular electrode pair of width 3 cm and length 3 cm. This notation is used consistently throughout the manuscript and Supporting Information.

We build on this strategy by presenting a textile stretch sensor in which longitudinal textile deformation is converted into a lateral shear overlap change between two conductive textile electrodes (see Figure 1a,b). In our design, the mechanically deforming textile elements are separated from the electrically active electrodes: stretch occurs primarily in the elastic textile regions, while the conductive electrodes are mounted on comparatively non-stretching textile panels and sense motion through a change in relative overlap. This mechanical–electrical decoupling preserves textile integration while reducing the need to repeatedly elongate the conductive sensing elements, which is particularly important for subtle body movements such as thoracic and abdominal breathing.

We validate the fidelity of our sensor design through a series of experiments, documenting the stretch response, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and cycle life of prototype sensor implementations. We also validate the accuracy of the designed sensors using a precise motion tracking system. Results indicate that the proposed design leads to a higher fidelity sensor compared to other fabric stretch sensors presented in the literature [22, 23, 30]. Furthermore, to demonstrate the sensor’s utility, we show that it maintains strong performance when placed on the body. Finally, we share example readings of the sensor used as a detector of breath and various body movements. We also deployed the sensors to measure breath at the abdomen and mid-back. The design, prototyping, and final integration of the sensors in a corset are shown in Figure 1d(i–iii), respectively. This deployment shows the flexibility of our e-Textile sensors in supporting multiple wearable configurations and measurement contexts.

Breath monitoring was selected as the primary motivating application because thoracic and abdominal breathing produce subtle textile motion and garment deformation that are challenging for many conventional e-Textile strain sensors to capture reliably. We also show two other applications of the sensor in the rest of the paper. Although pressure and body coupling influence the measured capacitance during wearable deployment, the intended sensing modality remains stretch sensing rather than direct pressure sensing.

Our contributions are as follows: (1) general design considerations for optimizing e-Textile sensor designs, (2) a novel capacitive stretch sensor design implementing these considerations, and (3) an evaluation of these designs highlighting how electrical and fabric considerations affect the behavior and quality of such sensors.

Design A emphasizes material stabilization, structural control, and long-term performance through the use of bonded composites, non-stretch substrates, and spacer fabrics that isolate deformation from the sensing elements. Its fabrication method prioritizes consistency, softness, and durability, but requires specialized materials and precise bonding steps. In contrast, Design B explores a simplified and more accessible fabrication approach, substituting highly engineered textiles with thinner, less compliant, and more readily available materials. This design reduces structural complexity and insulation thickness, aiming to produce a sensor that is less influenced by normal force and easier to construct, while intentionally trading off some material control and compressibility.

For all in vitro measurements, we used the setup shown in Figure 2b. This setup enabled precise and automatic stretching of the sensors without human interference. In this section, we present the detailed results of the in vitro and in vivo experiments. All sensor identifiers below follow the sensor nomenclature defined in the Introduction.

To quantify the linearity of the capacitance-displacement response, we fitted the mean stretch and release curves of each sensor variant with a linear model, 𝐶(𝑥) = 𝛽0 + 𝛽1𝑥, where 𝐶is capacitance and 𝑥is displacement. 𝑅2 was calculated for each phase and is reported in Table S1. The quantitative analysis shows that the effect of the rt electrode geometry depends on sensor scale and textile construction. For Design A, rt geometry improved the linearity metrics for the 3 × 3 and 5 × 3 sensors, but not for the 1 × 3 sensor. In particular, rt-5 × 3-A showed the most linear response among the Design A variants, with 𝑅2 = 0.9969 during stretch, and 𝑅2 = 0.9967 during release. In contrast, rt-1 × 3-A showed lower linearity than rr-1 × 3-A, indicating that the geometric correction is not universal at smaller electrode sizes. For Design B, the rt geometry improved 𝑅2 compared to the rr geometry in both stretch and release. During stretch, rr-3 × 3-B and rt-3 × 3-B exhibited 𝑅2 values of 0.9129 and 0.9686, respectively. During release, rr-3 × 3-B and rt-3 × 3-B exhibited 𝑅2 values of 0.9338 and 0.9631, respectively. These results support the interpretation that rt electrodes can compensate for curvature- or pressure-induced nonlinearities when out-of-plane deformation is sufficiently controlled, but that this effect can be masked by textile thickness and spacer texture.

These results indicate that the rt electrode geometry imposes the intended nonlinear overlap area function, but that the measured capacitance cannot be explained by in-plane overlap area alone. Deviations from the ideal geometric prediction are most pronounced in the smallest Design A sensor and are likely caused by scale-dependent edge effects, spacer texture, local electrode misalignment, and out-of-plane deformation of the textile. This suggests that the present triangular electrode design is one useful geometric compensation strategy, but not necessarily the only one: other, more complex geometries can achieve better linearization and could potentially outperform the current approach. Future work can explore such alternative electrode layouts and assess how they interact with textile mechanics and pressure-dependent deformation.

To validate the performance and accuracy of our sensors, we measured their capacitances in 100 cycles of stretch and release, together with the displacements of the electrodes on each other, using a high-resolution motion tracking system. Blue-colored solid lines and red-colored dashed lines represent capacitance and displacement measurements, respectively. There is a very good fit between the capacitance measurements from our e-Textile sensors and the displacement measurements from the motion tracking system.

The results of the breathing detection experiments are presented in Figure 4a (the second part of In Vivo 1). We defined seven breathing intervals (exhale hold, normal breath, inhale hold, deep breath, exhale hold, normal breath, exhale hold) for the participant and asked her to perform each interval for 10 s. Yellow, light blue, white, and pastel pink show the intervals for exhale hold, normal breath, inhale hold, and deep breath, respectively. The black and green colored curves show the normalized capacitances for the sensor with long (i) and short (ii) straps, respectively. The sensor with the shorter strap size exhibits higher capacitances than the sensor with the longer strap size. As shown in Figure S11, in one trial, the participant mixed the intervals, leading to some misalignment in the sensor data for the sensor with two strap sizes.

To evaluate the measurement accuracy of the motion tracking system, a static validation experiment was conducted using a calibrated wand equipped with four markers at known distances. The wand was positioned within the measurement volume, and three independent recordings were acquired. For each recording, the distances between one reference marker and the remaining three markers were calculated and compared with their corresponding nominal values. The measurement error was quantified using the root-mean-square (RMS) error between the measured and reference distances. Across all measurements, the overall RMS error was 0.0056 mm, indicating micrometer distance measurement accuracy of the motion tracking system.

3.3 Hysteresis

Across participants, the sensor maintained stable signal behavior for all measurements despite variations in body shape, garment tension, and sensor placement. In particular, respiration-related capacitance patterns remained clearly distinguishable across participants and activities, while dynamic activities such as walking and jogging produced consistent periodic responses corresponding to gait-related body motion. The extended duration measurements in In Vivo 3 demonstrated that the sensor maintained stable operation during continuous wearable use over several minutes without signal collapse or loss of sensitivity.

Hysteresis reduces repeatability in dynamic sensing applications. Across the tested range, the proposed design shows smaller differences between stretch and release curves than prior textile stretch sensors (see Figure 2c,d and Figure 3d), indicating reduced hysteresis and improved consistency. Remaining differences between stretch and release are most apparent in some Design A sensors and are likely explained by the relative stiffness of the sensing layers. During release, a small increase in the distance between the electrodes can occur, leading to a reduction in capacitance.
3.4 Cycle Life

We also observed that the absolute capacitance offset and signal amplitude varied between participants and placements, which is expected for wearable capacitive sensors because body morphology, textile tension, local curvature, and sensor pre-strain influence both electrode overlap and body coupling. Therefore, the proposed sensor should be interpreted as a calibrated wearable sensing platform whose deployment-specific response depends on garment integration and placement conditions.
3 Discussion

Cycle life measurements highlight the benefit of decoupling mechanical strain from the sensing electrodes. In particular, Design A maintains stable capacitance responses over repeated stretch–release cycles after an initial settling period (see Figure 3b and Figures S3–S7). In contrast, Design B shows reduced longterm stability, likely caused by the use of off-the-shelf stretch fabrics (see Figure 3b(ii) and Figure S8).

Current e-Textile sensors in the literature often exhibit nonlinear behavior across a wide range of displacements. They are generally designed to capture large motions and frequently degrade under repeated strain. Moreover, the performance of these sensors heavily depends on parameters such as material type and cutting techniques, which in turn rely on the designer’s expertise and precision.

Taken together, these characteristics support the use of the proposed sensor for reliable monitoring of subtle movements in wearable contexts. To demonstrate the practical robustness of the system, we deployed the sensor in a custom corset used by a vocalist as part of an experimental interactive performance platform (see Figure 1d).
3.5 Effects of Sensor Geometry

Our evaluation suggests that separating the mechanically deforming elements of the sensor from the electrically active sensing elements improves measurement quality for subtle on-body movements. Relative to prior textile stretch sensors, the proposed design shows improved linearity, high signal-to-noise ratios, reduced hysteresis, and stable cycle life behavior. At the same time, the sensor is optimized for small displacements and is not intended to replace designs that target larger ranges of motion.
3.1 Linearity

In the same way that material properties influence design choices, the effects of these design choices, and in turn, the materials themselves, are reflected in the data collected during sensor evaluations.
3.6.1 Electrode Design

In both designs, the sensing electrodes almost act as rigid islands connected by a compliant shear layer, analogous to an island– bridge structure in stretchable electronics. Under axial stretch, most deformation is taken up by the soft spacer/bridge, so the electrode pads themselves undergo significantly less elongation than the bulk. This is consistent with prior studies where conductive islands “ride along” on a deforming substrate [34, 35]. For example, in Ref. [35], lithographically defined islands protected a brittle electrode by letting it slide on stretchable bridges, avoiding local strain. Similarly, our pad electrode is largely decoupled from the garment stretch. We therefore expect the local strain (and stress) in the pad to be much lower than in a fully bonded design, improving the mechanical robustness of the sensing area.
3.6.2 Strap Design

Multiple effects of materials are apparent in the signal response curves. Looking at the response curves for Design A (Figure 2d), we see multiple instances where the signal does not immediately decrease, or where it increases before it decreases. When moving over a curved surface, this difference in thickness sometimes caused a slight lifting of the top element relative to the bottom, which prevented the sensor from reaching its theoretical maximum capacitance, or even reducing its capacitance reading toward the end of its active range.

5.1 Sensor Design and Implementation
In this section, we first provide the general design considerations and our construction method. Then, we proceed to discuss the specific implementations.
5.1.1 General Principles

Respiration monitoring was selected as the primary target application because thoracic and abdominal breathing produce relatively small textile deformations that are difficult to capture reliably using many conventional textile strain sensors. The additional body location measurements demonstrate that the sensing principle is more general and can support broader wearable movement monitoring applications beyond respiration alone.

We propose a two-layered mechanical capacitive e-Textile sensor with a shearing motion for measuring stretch in on-body applications. Two overlaid straps with a centrally aligned electrode of opposing sections of stretch and non-stretch materials create a shearing motion when strain is applied (Figure 1b). The design leverages the positive curvature of the body with the tension of the non-active stretch materials to stabilize the structure.
5.1.2 Design Considerations

Larger body movements, such as high amplitude elbow or knee flexion, shoulder motion, trunk bending, or large changes in garment circumference during vigorous activity, can impose strains and local textile displacements that exceed the tested 15 mm range. Prior wearable textile strain-sensing work for elbow and knee monitoring has therefore used sensors designed for substantially larger strain ranges, for example, flexion measurements within approximately 30% strain [40]. Similarly, wearable respiration systems evaluated during walking, running, or stair climbing highlight that dynamic activities can introduce larger garment deformation and motion artifacts than quiet breathing [41].

Beyond the technological functionality of the system, for a technological system to become wearable, the design should include properties such as the ability to adapt to the varied shape of bodies, match with human abilities, and finally be deployable in everyday use and socially acceptable [42]. In the present work, we optimize a sensor for optimal deployability in everyday garments by optimizing the design to adapt to and move with the body. Such optimization, in turn, leads to better technological functionality, enabling the sensor to precisely measure subtle human behaviors.

For applications requiring larger displacement ranges, the proposed mechano-capacitive principle can be scaled in several ways. First, the electrode length can be increased so that a larger shear displacement can occur before the electrode overlap becomes too small for reliable capacitance measurement. Second, the mechanical textile linkage can be redesigned so that a larger garment extension is converted into a smaller electrode displacement, for example, by increasing the length of the stretch region, adding compliant intermediate textile sections, or using multiple stretch zones in series. Third, multiple sensors can be distributed across a garment so that large body motion is measured as the sum of several smaller local displacements rather than by a single sensor operating over its full travel. Finally, the sensor can be pre-positioned or pre-strained so that the expected motion occurs near the center of the calibrated range, where the capacitance response remains most reliable.

In addition, since the sensing element is continuously mechanically manipulated as the fabric deforms, the deformation of sensing materials causes fatigue, hysteresis, and general instability in longitudinal readings [23]. We address this issue by applying a design strategy that creates a separation between the mechanical moving parts of the sensor and its electrical parts. This is achieved by combining non-stretch (woven) with stretch (knit) elements in such a way that the place at which the fabric is stretched is carefully chosen and controlled, enabling sensing materials to be placed in areas that are not stretched.

The conductive electrode fabric is first bonded by “tacking” it to the double-sided adhesive film in a sheet, and the electrodes are then precisely cut with raw edges. The spacer fabric is then applied over the conductive fabric electrodes to ensure insulation and to protect the electrodes from degradation/oxidation caused by sweat or ambient moisture.
